t: Minimum Skips to Arrive at Meeting On Time — Trading Rests for Deadlines
o: You traverse n roads at a fixed speed, and after each road except the last you must idle until the next whole hour — unless you spend one of your limited skips to leave immediately. Minimize the number of skips needed so the total arrival time is at most hoursBefore, or return -1. Example 1: dist = [1,3,2], speed = 4, hoursBefore = 2 — resting after every road lands you at 2.5h, but skipping the first rest makes road 2 finish exactly on the hour and the trip ends at 1.5h, so the answer is 1. Example 2: dist = [7,3,5,5], speed = 2, hoursBefore = 10 needs the rests after roads 1 and 3 skipped, arriving exactly at 10. Example 3 has speed = 1: every road takes a whole number of hours, rests never waste anything, and no skip count helps — answer -1. Every travel time is dist[i]/speed hours, so multiplying hours by speed turns all quantities into integers and ceiling rounding into exact arithmetic.
k: Scale time by speed: road i costs dist[i] scaled units and a rest rounds up to the next multiple of speed — pure integer math with no floating point error.
A skip propagates: leaving road i unrounded shifts every later departure, but (next road, skips used) is still a sufficient state.
Feasibility grows monotonically with skips, so the answer is simply the smallest k whose DP row lands within hoursBefore * speed.

a.i: Testing whether k skips suffice means DFS-ing every combination of rest/skip decisions while tracking the scaled arrival time; feasibility is monotone in k, so probe k = 0, 1, 2, ... and stop at the first success. Prune any branch already past the deadline. Two branches per road over n = 1000 roads is astronomically large — this baseline exists to expose the overlapping subproblems that DP will cache.
s: Work in scaled units: limit = hoursBefore * speed.
For each candidate k from 0 upward, run a feasibility DFS holding (road i, arrival t, skips left).
At each road add dist[i]; prune if t exceeds limit; succeed on finishing the last road within limit.
Branch: skip the following rest (consume a skip, keep t exact) or round t up to the next multiple of speed.
Return the first feasible k, or -1 if none.
a.t: O(2^n) — two branches per road, re-run for each candidate skip count.

a.n: Approach 2: Dynamic Programming over Roads and Skips
a.i: Let dp[j] be the minimal scaled arrival time at the current frontier having used exactly j skips, rebuilt road by road with a rolling row. Adding road d gives candidate t = dp[j] + d; resting rounds it up to a multiple of speed keeping j unchanged, skipping carries exact t into j+1. After processing everything, the first j with dp[j] <= hoursBefore * speed is optimal since extra skips can never hurt. n^2 states with O(1) transitions each — trivially fast for n <= 1000.
s: Initialize dp[0] = 0 and all other entries to infinity; set limit = hoursBefore * speed.
For each road d rebuild ndp from dp: candidate t = dp[j] + d.
Rest transition: ndp[j] gets t rounded up to the next multiple of speed; skip transition: ndp[j+1] gets exact t.
After the last road, return the smallest j with dp[j] <= limit, else -1.
a.t: O(n^2) — n roads times n+1 skip counts, constant work per cell.
a.sp: O(n) — two rolling rows of skip counts.

w: Lead with the scaling trick in an interview — floating-point ceilings are the classic silent killer here because accumulated fractional error can flip a rounding boundary. Pitfalls: skipping after the last road is legal but pointless (the loop tolerates it), j never needs to exceed n-1 meaningfully, and hoursBefore * speed reaches 10^13 so C++/Java need 64-bit while JS doubles stay safe under 2^53. Follow-ups: reconstruct the actual plan with parent pointers, or generalize to per-road speeds (same DP, per-road scale factor).
